questions.question: Classify economic indicators by timing, with two correct examples of each type, and explain why unemployment belongs where it does.
questions.expected_answer: Leading indicators turn before the economy turns — building plans passed, job advertisements, factory orders, new vehicle sales, share prices; they anticipate activity because each represents an intention about the future, and the Reserve Bank compiles a composite leading indicator that bends months ahead of the cycle. Coincident indicators move with the cycle — industrial production, retail sales, real GDP — reporting where the economy stands right now. Lagging indicators confirm a turning point only after it has passed — unemployment, inventories, insolvencies. Unemployment lags because employers retrench late in a downturn, hoping the dip passes, and rehire cautiously in a recovery, waiting for certainty; employment therefore moves last, and a falling unemployment rate certifies a recovery that is already old rather than predicting one. A complete answer adds the two supporting disciplines: keep the level of an indicator apart from its rate of change, and convert nominal readings to real by stripping out inflation — nominal growth of 7,5 percent under 5,5 percent inflation is real growth of only about 2 percent.

questions.question: Explain why economic indicators alone cannot judge a country's development, and show how life expectancy, infant mortality, the HDI and the Gini coefficient complete the picture, using South African values where relevant.
questions.expected_answer: Economic indicators measure the machine — production, prices, money, trade — but say nothing about whether growth reaches human lives; GDP can rise while people sicken, and GDP per capita can fall while GDP grows if population grows faster. Social indicators measure the passengers. Life expectancy at birth compresses nutrition, healthcare, water and safety into one number — South Africa's collapsed during the untreated-AIDS years and recovered by more than a decade once antiretroviral treatment was rolled out, showing policy appearing in a statistic within a generation. Infant mortality — deaths before the first birthday per thousand live births — is the sharpest poverty gauge because the youngest die first when water, food and clinics fail. Education gauges must measure learning, not just enrolment, and service indicators — piped water, sanitation, electricity, with electrification now reaching roughly nine households in ten — are development a household can touch. The HDI blends life expectancy, education and income per person into one score between 0 and 1, dethroning GDP as the sole scoreboard. The Gini coefficient measures how income is shared, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person holds everything); South Africa's, around 0,63 to 0,65, is among the highest recorded, meaning strong economic gauges can coexist with extreme inequality.

questions.question: A magazine article ranks countries by total GDP converted at market exchange rates. Identify three corrections an economist would demand before trusting the ranking as a comparison of living standards, and distinguish the roles of the IMF and the World Bank in international economic life.
questions.expected_answer: Correction one: divide by population — total GDP measures a country's weight, not its people's wellbeing; China's total dwarfs Switzerland's while the average Swiss resident is far richer, so per-capita figures are the minimum standard. Correction two: convert at purchasing power parity, not market exchange rates — money buys more at home in poorer countries (R100 buys a meal, a ride and change locally while its converted equivalent barely buys a coffee in London), so market-rate conversion understates poor countries' real living standards, sometimes by half or more; the table must declare its conversion method. Correction three: remember coverage — official statistics miss the informal sector, subsistence production and unpaid household work, all proportionally larger in poorer countries, so measured gaps overstate true gaps, and definitions such as unemployment differ across borders. The institutions: both were created at Bretton Woods in 1944. The IMF is the short-term crisis lender — it monitors member economies and lends to countries in balance-of-payments trouble, attaching conditionality to its loans, as when South Africa drew about 4,3 billion dollars in the 2020 pandemic. The World Bank is the long-term development financier — patient loans and expertise for infrastructure, education and health, and the publisher of much comparative data. One line: the IMF stabilises crises; the World Bank funds development.
